title: TCAD Based Study of String Current Variability in 3D NAND Flash Memory
problem: Process variations during etching, deposition, and lithography cause significant variability in string current and electrical properties of 3D NAND flash memory cells, impacting device performance and reliability at advanced technology nodes.
motivation: As memory cell sizes shrink and cell densities increase, precise control over fabrication parameters is crucial for maintaining performance and reliability. Uncontrolled variability threatens the scalability and cost-efficiency benefits of 3D NAND technology.
method: The researchers used TCAD simulations (a tool that models how semiconductors work electrically) to test how manufacturing variations affect 3D NAND memory cells. They changed key dimensions—cell spacing, oxide layer thicknesses, channel thickness, and plug depth—and measured how each change affected the string current (the electrical current flowing through the memory cell) and related electrical properties such as voltage thresholds and gain. This reveals which manufacturing imperfections have the biggest impact on memory performance and reliability.
key_novelty: This work systematically analyzes how manufacturing process variations affect 3D NAND string current and related electrical properties (ion current, threshold voltage, gain, and subthreshold swing) using TCAD simulation.
contributions: Quantified impact of process variations on 3D NAND electrical parameters: 20% variation causes ~78% Ion deviation, 21% Vth deviation, 38% Gm deviation, 14% SS deviation
Identified cell spacing as critical parameter with significant impact vs. plug depth with negligible effect
Demonstrated need for variability-aware design strategies in advanced 3D NAND
limitations: TCAD simulation only; lacks experimental validation on fabricated devices
Limited to 3D NAND architecture; findings may not generalize to 2D or other memory types
Does not propose mitigation strategies or design techniques
